title: Menopause at Work: How Employers Can Support Women
description: How employers can support women through menopause at work: practical policies, workplace adjustments and conversations that retain talent.
lead: Menopause affects many working women, impacting productivity and well-being. Companies like HSBC India are normalizing menopause through awareness, support, and workplace adjustments to better accommodate affected employees.
imageAlt: Menopause at Work: How Employers Can Support Women
html:
“We understand that menopause will have a direct or indirect impact on everyone at some point. We want all colleagues to feel understood and supported, as well as equipped to support others who are going through menopause. Hence, it is important for us to normalise menopause,” said Archana Chadha, Head of Human Resources, HSBC India.

Menopause is when a woman’s periods stop due to lower hormone levels. It occurs when menstruation ends, and it involves a drop in estrogen levels. It usually happens between the ages of 45 and 55, but can also be earlier or later. The average age for a woman to go through menopause is 51. It can be earlier than this, naturally or due to surgery, or illness. Some women sail through their menopause with barely a symptom, but it’s not an easy transition for all. And symptoms may start years before menopause, during the perimenopause phase. According to the Faculty of Occupational Medicine (FOM), nearly 8 out of 10 menopausal women are in work. 3 out of 4 women experience symptoms, 1 in 4 could experience serious symptoms. One in three of the workforces will soon be over 50, and retirement ages are now 68. 

The Gennev survey found that symptoms that most impacted work productivity included sleep disturbances (80%), mood changes (78%), anxiety (75%), brain fog/cognitive issues (75%) and joint pain (52%). 

Some other symptoms vary greatly, and commonly include (but aren’t limited to):

  1.  Hot flushes
  2.  Night sweats
  3.  Dizziness
  4.  Fatigue
  5.  Memory loss
  6.  Depression
  7.  Headaches
  8.  Joint stiffness, aches and pains
  9.  Reduced concentration
  10.  Heavy periods

By talking about it openly, raising awareness and putting the right support in place, perhaps we could get to a point where menopause is no longer an issue in the workplace at all. 

Menopause symptoms can have a significant impact on women at work. Research by the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development found that two thirds (67%) of working women between the ages of 40 and 60 with experience of menopausal symptoms said they have had a mostly negative impact on them at work. Let’s talk about its impact:

  • 79% said they were less able to concentrate
  • 68% said they experienced more stress
  • nearly half (49%) said they felt less patient with clients and colleagues, and
  • 46% felt less physically able to carry out work tasks.

As a result of this, over half of respondents were able to think of a time when they were unable to go into work due to their menopause symptoms.

How workplace adjustments could attract and retain valued employees suffering from menopause:

  1. Employers should consider providing rest areas or Quiet Rooms. 
  2. Employers should consider setting up Cool Rooms for women suffering from hot splashes.
  3. Employers should support women by allowing them to wear cooler clothing.
  4. Promoting flexibility will also help women experiencing menopausal symptoms. Employers may allow women to work from home where possible.
  5. Sickness or Paid Leave should be given to the employees suffering from menopause.
  6. A dedicated HR menopause champion should be provided for the women in the organization experiencing menopause so that they can talk to them.
  7. A key to support employees is to have open conversations about menopause so that women can ask for adjustments in their work.
  8. Employers can support women by introducing a menopause policy that outlines the support available and provides guidance to managers and colleagues.

Let’s see which companies have already taken steps to support their female employees during menopause-

Standard Chartered Bank

They have introduced toolkits, conversation guides and counselling support, as well as e-learning and internal events. Employees experiencing the menopause are also well supported by flexible working policies and workplace adjustments to help them better manage their symptoms.

Adobe

Employees, their partners or spouses have complimentary access to Peppy Menopause and Peppy Fertility services including one-to-one access to experts, online resources or moderated group chats.

Microsoft

It provides counselling and hormone therapy access to their employees in order to address menopause.

Organon

They provide menopausal leave, keeping managers informed about the issue, and implementing a range of practices aimed at destigmatizing the topic, such as giving employees a space to take a quick break during a hot flash or providing a desk fan.

Organisations including HSBC India, IBM, HUL, NatWest Group and Intuit are trying to normalise menopause through a raft of initiatives: from raising awareness; enhancing medical coverage to cover menopause and providing access to doctors/ menopause specialists and mental health support, leaves and flexible work policies to help women employees navigate this stressful time.

HUL has assimilated its initiatives on menopause within the larger umbrella of equitable policies.“At HUL, our equitable policy approach ensures that we support our employees across all life stages. Our flexible work options, group medical insurance, and unlimited sick leaves cater to all diverse needs, including that of women going through menopause, said Anuradha Razdan, Executive Director, HR, HUL

title: The Essential Guide to Enhancing Gender Diversity in Your Workplace
description: A practical guide to improving gender diversity at work: hiring, retention, policies and culture changes that help women thrive and progress.
lead: Gender diversity means fair representation of all genders in organizations, improving profitability, innovation, and employee satisfaction. It’s essential for attracting top talent and fostering an inclusive work environment.
imageAlt: The Essential Guide to Enhancing Gender Diversity in Your Workplace
html:
We live in an era where companies are proud to stand (virtually) and say “we want to be better with gender diversity, equity, and inclusion” such that even “gender diversity” has become a buzzword. So let us first comprehend the essence of gender diversity and why it is so critical.

Gender diversity refers to the equitable representation of all genders within an organization, including men, women, transgender, and non-binary individuals. The goal is to remove barriers to accessing all types of employment services that are based on gender.

Workplace equality without respect to gender identification sustains the premise that individuals are compensated, promoted and hired based on their qualifications, not because of their sexuality. One of the many benefits of gender equality is that it does more than just increase workplace inclusion and diversity. Employees tend to be happier and more satisfied in a gender-balanced environment.

According to research, workers are more likely to be committed to their jobs and experience higher levels of job satisfaction when they believe that their gender does not limit their prospects for growth and success. Moreover, gender equality regarding paid maternity leaves and leaves from work have minimized stress levels and increased the general sense of well-being. The more competitive the organization for human capital, the more important it is to create a friendly work environment. Age, ethnicity, and race diversity help a great deal. Organizations strive to increase the representation of a diverse mix of people in their workforce. 

The Benefits of Gender Diversity for the Company-

Increases Profitability and Production: There are many ways in which gender-neutral workforces do better. A more integrated and efficient team is among the primary advantages due to higher gender equality in the workforce. Diversity of thought encourages a more holistic approach and, thereby, more remarkable outcomes. Encouragement of an atmosphere where employees of all stripes are welcome can result in a dramatic rise in business growth.

Enhances Talent Retention: Almost 39% of the employees think about the organization as more inclusive compared to that in which they are working presently. Improvement in gender diversity at the workplace will lead to increasing satisfaction among employees and hence retention. This suggests that employees are more likely to stay longer with a company and do their jobs more effectively because of variableness. Equal opportunities for both men and women in the workforce can make the company stand out in front of potential top talent and not just increase employee retention.

Innovation and Creativity: Different perspectives are invariably the reason for innovation. Having women as part of the workforce is shown to approach problems in an innovative way. According to research by Harvard Business Review, having more gender parity at workplaces will lead to 19% more innovative revenues.

The Benefits of Gender Diversity for the Employees-

Builds a Safe Environment: The employees working in a gender-diverse environment are more tolerant to other people's opinions. This ensures that all employees, irrespective of their gender identity, are free to air their views without fear of being judged. In addition, everybody feels valued and at home due to the appreciation of all.

Content Employees: Engaged and motivated teams are happier and more content in their work and work environment. Motivated teams positively impact other teams in the organization, improve employee engagement, and help raise overall organizational morale.

Flexibility: Everyone feels welcomed and has equal possibilities to progress in a varied team and inclusive corporate culture. When a company treats all of its employees equally, regardless of differences, it fosters flexibility and enhances the work environment.

Bridging this gap requires that organizations make equality a clear objective, along with any other business objective. Business leaders have to engender in themselves and their employees a culture of safe interaction to the extent that subjects such as inequality can be discussed with sincerity. It becomes crucial for employers to curate policies and initiatives which are convenient for women. For example: 

  • Flexible working hours with hybrid work culture, 
  • Comprehensive parental leave,
  • Lactation rooms, 
  • Women's health benefits, for example, coverage for specific health needs like mammograms, fertility treatments, and menopause support,
  • Strong, clearly communicated policies against sexual harassment and discrimination, 
  • Career path flexibility, options for non-linear career progression that accommodate life changes.

Companies have to outline major actions they themselves can do to drive meaningful change. It's time to forever close the gender gap and realize the potential a world has been losing out on for so many centuries. In other words, it becomes both a moral duty and good business sense to enforce gender diversity at the workplace. Thus, companies committed to equality and inclusiveness benefit from an increased talent supply, varied perspectives, smoother collaboration groups, increased rate of retention in employees, engaged customers, better recruitment, reputation, and at last, deeper profitability.

title: Tips for Women Re-Entering the Workforce after a Career Break
description: Returning to work after a break is possible with confidence, updated resumes, networking, and interview preparation. Family support and focus on goals are key.
lead: Returning to work after a break is possible with confidence, updated resumes, networking, and interview preparation. Family support and focus on goals are key.
imageAlt: Tips for Women Re-Entering the Workforce after a Career Break
html:
After serving as the First Lady of the United States, Michelle Obama took a break to focus on her family and personal projects. She later returned to public life as an author and advocate, inspiring many with her memoir "Becoming" and her continued activism. Similarly, before achieving fame as the author of the Harry Potter series, J.K. Rowling took a break from her career after facing numerous personal challenges, including divorce and single motherhood. She returned to writing and created one of the most successful book series of all time.

Like them, do you want to resume your career after being among the numerous women who took a temporary leave? You are not alone, though. Due to the high cost of child care and a general lack of acceptable maternity leave, many women take temporary breaks from their careers to care for their young children. In reality, the main reason women take temporary leave from their jobs is to care for family members. Many of these women may want to return to work at a later stage of their life, but it is not always easy. A career gap can become a challenging barrier for any job seeker. There’s always a dilemma in women whether to keep financial, family or personal needs first.

Here are some tips to keep in mind before making a comeback in your career-

Show Confidence: Don't feel apologetic or embarrassed about your career break. Don't undermine its value. Even family commitments such as elderly care and child care stand as warranted. If you lost your job and went back to studying, tell them about it. It is easy for women in our society not to think of working and contributing, but that thought shouldn't come into your mind. You need to bring out the confidence in you at your interview. That your resume has a small gap doesn't mean you are not as good as the next capable candidate.

Build Professional Connections: Note opportunities to join professional associations, network, and attend industry-specific conferences that will present you with an opportunity to learn something new or hear from individuals with similar interests. Expanding your network introduces you to those who will either become a hiring manager themselves, know someone that is hiring, serve as a reference for you in your job search, or become mentors who can help guide you on your job search.

Rework on Your Resume: Your confidence should be reflected in your resume too, so rework on your resume to make sure it conveys your belief in yourself. Also, make sure it uses current industry terminologies and emphasizes any previous skill sets that are still in demand. To do so, take a look at job qualifications on a job-listing site to learn what employers are looking for today and how those line up with your past experience. Then, rewrite your resume accordingly.

Prepare for Your Interview: Another way to secure a return to work is by nailing a great interview. You can prepare for this by practicing answers to questions about your absence. As you develop your answer, include what you're doing during your career break, and consider explaining why you made that choice. Get insight into the areas of your field that have changed, so you will know how and where to brush up your knowledge. Help the hiring manager be confident in you as a strong candidate for the role by projecting confidence in your responses.

Stay Focused: One of the first steps in returning to work is to assess your situation and focus on your needs. Review your education and experience, but also think about your skills, interests, strengths and what you value most in a new position and an employer. Keep in mind that both your interests and your skills may have changed since last you were employed. By focusing on what you want from a new position and narrowing down your job search to fit, you'll minimize the risk that you'll job-hop and maximize the potential for happiness in your new role.

Support from Family: Family and partner support is crucial for women re-entering the workforce after a career break. It offers emotional encouragement that boosts confidence and helps combat self-doubt. Practical assistance with household chores and childcare allows women to focus on their job search and transition smoothly. Additionally, leveraging family and partner networks can create job opportunities and professional introductions, making the return to work more effective and less stressful.

Although going back to work after a professional break may seem difficult, it is a brave step that is worthwhile. Women may effectively relaunch their professional careers despite the genuine obstacles they face if they adopt the correct mindset, make smart plans, and consistently work on improving themselves. Recognize that the workforce values variety and the distinct viewpoints and experiences that women can offer. After a professional sabbatical, going back to work is a journey that calls for bravery, tenacity, and planning. Women must accept the events that have shaped them during their sabbatical and acknowledge their value as they take on the challenge of re-entering the workforce. Women can successfully return to work and create doors to new and rewarding opportunities by heeding this advice and remaining proactive.
